words.definition: Similar in some respects to something else, so a useful comparison can be drawn.
words.example: The heart is analogous to a pump, pushing fluid through a network of pipes.
words.mnemonic: ana- ('according to') + logos ('ratio') → things in the same proportion; like an analog clock mirroring a digital one.

words.definition: So fundamentally unlike as to have almost nothing in common.
words.example: The festival somehow united disparate crowds—metalheads, grandmothers, and toddlers.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'dis-SEPARATE': things set firmly apart from one another.

words.definition: Similar enough in size or quality to be reasonably measured against each other.
words.example: Their salaries are comparable, though one of them works in a far bigger city.
words.mnemonic: Say 'com-PAIR-able': you can pair the two up as near equals.

words.definition: Closely related or similar in nature or character.
words.example: The dull ache in his chest was akin to homesickness, though he had never left home.
words.mnemonic: A-KIN: your kin are family, and things akin to each other are 'family'—closely related.

words.definition: Equal in seriousness or effect to something else, though not literally identical.
words.example: Walking out of the meeting was tantamount to resigning on the spot.
words.mnemonic: 'Tant-AMOUNT': it comes to the same amount—picture two mountains of equal height.

words.definition: Equal in value, meaning, or function to something else.
words.example: A mile is roughly equivalent to 1.6 kilometers.
words.mnemonic: equi- ('equal') + -valent (from valere, 'to be worth') → of equal worth.

words.definition: Made up of parts that are all of the same kind or nature.
words.example: The suburb was strikingly homogeneous—every house beige, every lawn trimmed to the same height.
words.mnemonic: homo- ('same') + genus ('kind'); think 'homogenized milk,' stirred until every part is identical.

words.definition: Made up of parts that are of many different kinds or natures.
words.example: New York's heterogeneous population speaks more than two hundred languages.
words.mnemonic: hetero- ('different') + genus ('kind') → different kinds; the opposite of homogenized.

words.definition: A noticeable, often unfair, difference between two or more things.
words.example: The disparity between executive pay and worker wages keeps widening every year.
words.mnemonic: dis- ('not') + parity ('equality') → not on par, off-even.

words.definition: An inconsistency between two things that are supposed to match.
words.example: The auditor flagged a discrepancy between the receipts and the ledger totals.
words.mnemonic: Picture 'dis-CREPE-ancy': two crepes that don't stack evenly because they don't agree.

words.definition: Moving or developing in different directions; growing increasingly unlike each other.
words.example: The twins held divergent views on nearly every subject, from politics to pizza toppings.
words.mnemonic: di- ('apart') + vergere ('to bend') → bending apart; picture a fork in the road splitting in two.

words.definition: To move toward and meet at a single common point.
words.example: Protesters converged on the capital from every corner of the country.
words.mnemonic: con- ('together') + vergere ('to bend') → bending together; think of highway lanes merging into one.

words.definition: To separate and move in different directions from a shared starting point.
words.example: Two roads diverged in the wood, and the traveler paused, unsure which to take.
words.mnemonic: di- ('apart') + vergere ('to bend') → bending apart; the exact opposite of merge.

words.definition: To place two things side by side, often to highlight their contrast.
words.example: The gallery juxtaposed a Renaissance portrait with a smartphone selfie on the same wall.
words.mnemonic: juxta- (Latin 'beside') + pose ('to place') → 'just-a-pose' the two right next to each other.

words.definition: A comparison between two things that points out a shared similarity.
words.example: She explained memory with an analogy: the brain is a library, and forgetting is a misfiled book.
words.mnemonic: ana- ('according to') + logos ('ratio') → a matching ratio: 'A is to B as C is to D.'

words.definition: Running side by side at a constant distance, or being similar and occurring at the same time.
words.example: The two hiking trails ran parallel to each other along the ridge.
words.mnemonic: The two 'l's in paral-l-el stand side by side like two parallel lines.

words.definition: The state of being equal, especially in amount, value, or status.
words.example: Workers demanded pay parity with colleagues doing identical jobs.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pair-ity' — a pair matched evenly on both sides.

words.definition: Not in harmony or keeping with the surroundings or with other things present.
words.example: The neon sign looked incongruous on the quiet medieval street.
words.mnemonic: In- (not) + congruous (fitting): something that simply does NOT fit.

words.definition: In agreement or matching; corresponding perfectly in shape or character.
words.example: Her actions were congruent with the values she preached.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'gru' echoes 'agree' — congruent things agree and line up.

words.definition: Always the same; not changing or varying in form or quality.
words.example: The bricks were baked to a uniform shade of red.
words.mnemonic: Uni- (one) + form: one single form all the way through.

words.definition: A noticeable difference or contrast between similar things.
words.example: He drew a sharp distinction between being confident and being arrogant.
words.mnemonic: Di-STINCT-ion: what is distinct clearly stands apart from the rest.

words.definition: To recognize or express what makes two or more things unlike each other.
words.example: A good sommelier can differentiate wines by a single sip.
words.mnemonic: To spot the 'different' bits buried inside the word.

words.definition: To perceive or point out one thing as separate from another.
words.example: In the fog, she could barely distinguish the shoreline from the sky.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'extinguish' — you extinguish confusion by telling things apart.

words.definition: To perceive or detect something that is not immediately obvious.
words.example: Through the static, he could just discern a faint voice.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'cernere', to sift — you sift the truth out of the noise.

words.definition: To recognize a fine difference between things, or to treat groups unequally and unjustly.
words.example: A trained ear can discriminate between nearly identical musical tones.
words.mnemonic: At its worst, 'dis-CRIMINATE' treats a whole group like criminals.

words.definition: A very slight, subtle difference in meaning, expression, or tone.
words.example: A skilled translator captures every nuance of the original poem.
words.mnemonic: From Latin for 'cloud' — subtle shades that blend like clouds.

words.definition: A series of small, successive steps or stages between two extremes.
words.example: The painting showed a smooth gradation from deep blue to pale pink.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'grade' — like grades stepping down from A to F.

words.definition: A broad range of related qualities, ideas, or positions between two extremes.
words.example: Opinions on the issue cover the entire political spectrum.
words.mnemonic: Think of a rainbow's 'spectacle' of colors spread across a range.

words.definition: A division or contrast between two things that are opposed or entirely different.
words.example: The film explores the dichotomy between duty and desire.
words.mnemonic: Di- (two) + '-chotomy' (cut): a clean cut into two halves.

words.definition: A person or thing that is the direct opposite of another.
words.example: His calm patience was the antithesis of his brother's fiery temper.
words.mnemonic: Anti- (against) + thesis (position): a stance set squarely against another.

words.definition: A person or thing matching another in role or function within a different group.
words.example: The foreign minister met her counterpart from France to discuss the treaty.
words.mnemonic: counter + part — someone playing the matching part on the other side of the counter.

words.definition: Matching in size or degree; kept in proper balance with something else.
words.example: Her salary was finally commensurate with her years of experience.
words.mnemonic: com- (together) + measure — things measured together, in equal measure.

words.definition: Sized or scaled to match another thing in a fair, balanced way.
words.example: The punishment should be proportionate to the crime committed.
words.mnemonic: pro-PORTION — the right portion for the size, portions kept in balance.

words.definition: Too big or too small in comparison with something else; badly balanced.
words.example: He spent a disproportionate amount of time on one tiny detail.
words.mnemonic: dis- (not) + proportionate — not in proportion, tipped out of balance.

words.definition: A likeness or similarity between two people or things.
words.example: The resemblance between the twins was so strong that teachers confused them.
words.mnemonic: re-SEMBLE sounds like 'assemble' look-alikes — resemble = look alike.

words.definition: A natural liking for or attraction toward someone or something.
words.example: She had a strong affinity for cats and adopted three of them.
words.mnemonic: Think 'a-FIN' — two fish whose fins keep them swimming together, naturally drawn.

words.definition: A family bond, or a strong feeling of connection between people.
words.example: Meeting other survivors, he felt an instant kinship with them.
words.mnemonic: kin + ship — the 'ship' (bond) that holds your kin together.

words.definition: To match or be in agreement with something; also, to exchange letters.
words.example: The witness's account did not correspond with the video footage.
words.mnemonic: co- (together) + respond — two things respond together, so they match.

words.definition: To state the opposite of what someone says, or to be inconsistent with it.
words.example: The new evidence seemed to contradict everything the suspect had claimed.
words.mnemonic: contra- (against) + dict (speak) — to speak against.

words.definition: Having mixed or conflicting feelings toward something at the same time.
words.example: She felt ambivalent about the move, excited yet sad to leave home.
words.mnemonic: ambi- (both) + valent (strength/value) — pulled both ways at once.

words.definition: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than any clear reason.
words.example: The referee's arbitrary decision left both teams confused and angry.
words.mnemonic: An arbiter (judge) ruling on a whim — a moody arbiter's arbitrary call.

words.definition: Existing as a natural, permanent, and inseparable part of something.
words.example: There is an inherent risk in any extreme sport.
words.mnemonic: in-HERE-nt — the quality is 'in here,' built right into the thing.

words.definition: Belonging naturally to something; part of its essential, basic nature.
words.example: The intrinsic value of gold has nothing to do with its shine.
words.mnemonic: intr- (into/inside) — the worth is inside, built into the thing itself.

words.definition: Coming from outside something rather than being part of its basic nature.
words.example: Money is an extrinsic reward, while pride in the work comes from within.
words.mnemonic: ex- (out/external) — extrinsic comes from the exterior, the outside.

words.definition: Present from birth and natural, rather than learned or acquired.
words.example: Some people seem to have an innate talent for music.
words.mnemonic: in + nate (natus = born) — you were born with it, it's inborn.

words.definition: Seeming to be present everywhere at the same time; found in all places.
words.example: Smartphones have become so ubiquitous that it's rare to see anyone without one.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'ubique' (everywhere); think 'you-be-quick' to spot it — it's already all around you.

words.definition: Spreading widely and present in every part of something.
words.example: A pervasive smell of smoke seeped into every room of the house.
words.mnemonic: 'Per-' (through) + 'vade' (go): it goes through everything, like a fog per-vading a valley.

words.definition: Common or widespread in a particular place or at a particular time.
words.example: Colds are especially prevalent during the damp winter months.
words.mnemonic: 'Prevail' + '-ent': whatever prevails is what you'll see most often.

words.definition: Happening at irregular intervals; scattered and not constant.
words.example: Sporadic gunfire broke the night's silence, then long quiet stretches returned.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spores' scattered by a plant — landing here and there, unpredictably.

words.definition: A very great or countless number of things.
words.example: The clear night sky revealed a myriad of stars too numerous to count.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'myrias' (ten thousand); 'my-riad' sounds like 'my riot' — a riot of countless things.

words.definition: Stated or appearing to be true, though not necessarily so.
words.example: The ostensible reason for his visit was friendship, but he really came for money.
words.mnemonic: Root 'ostend' (to show); it's the version shown on the surface, not the real one underneath.

words.definition: Understood or implied without being directly expressed in words.
words.example: By staying silent when the plan was announced, she gave her tacit approval.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'tacitus' (silent), same root as 'taciturn' — an agreement made in silence.

words.definition: Suggested or understood though not directly stated.
words.example: There was an implicit warning in her tone, though she never actually threatened him.
words.mnemonic: 'Im-' (in) + 'plicit' (folded): the meaning is folded inside, not laid out on the surface.

words.definition: Stated clearly and in full detail, leaving no room for confusion.
words.example: The instructions were explicit: press the red button only in an emergency.
words.mnemonic: 'Ex-' (out) + 'plicit' (folded): everything unfolded and laid out in the open.

words.definition: Done or shown openly and not secretly.
words.example: His overt hostility was plain to everyone at the meeting.
words.mnemonic: 'Overt' = 'over the table' — out in the open where all can see it.

words.definition: Kept secret or hidden; not openly shown or acknowledged.
words.example: The agency ran a covert operation the public knew nothing about.
words.mnemonic: 'Covert' has 'cover' in it — something kept under cover.

words.definition: Done openly and unashamedly, in a way that offends.
words.example: The referee somehow missed a blatant foul that the whole stadium saw.
words.mnemonic: 'Blatant' sounds like 'blaring' — as loud and shameless as a blaring horn.

words.definition: So delicate or slight as to be hard to notice or describe.
words.example: There was a subtle shift in her expression that only close friends would catch.
words.mnemonic: The silent 'b' in 'subtle' is itself subtle — you barely notice it's there.

words.definition: Clearly visible and standing out so as to attract attention.
words.example: In her bright red coat, she was conspicuous among the crowd of gray suits.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-' + 'spic' (to look, as in 'spectacles'): everyone's eyes are drawn to look at it.

words.definition: Not clearly visible and not attracting attention.
words.example: He chose an inconspicuous corner table where no one would notice him.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) added to 'conspicuous' — think of a beige wall your eyes just slide past.

words.definition: Careful and tactful in what you say or do so as to avoid drawing attention.
words.example: She gave a discreet nod across the room so no one else would notice.
words.mnemonic: The two e's sit quietly side by side at the end — discreEt keeps a secret between them.

words.definition: Separate and individually distinct; not joined to others.
words.example: The course is split into five discrete modules, each with its own final exam.
words.mnemonic: discreTe = separaTe — the t keeps the two e's apart, each standing alone.

words.definition: More than is wanted or useful; beyond what a situation requires.
words.example: Once the point had been proven three times, any further argument felt superfluous.
words.mnemonic: super + fluous — a 'super flow' that overflows past what you actually need.

words.definition: No longer useful because it duplicates something already in place.
words.example: After the new system went live, the old backup server was redundant and switched off.
words.mnemonic: re-DONE-dant — it's been 'redone' so many times the extra copy is pointless.

words.definition: Not relevant to the matter at hand; coming from outside and unconnected.
words.example: The editor trimmed extraneous details that pulled the reader away from the main story.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'extra' — it's extra stuff from the outside, not part of the core.

words.definition: Directly relevant and clearly connected to the subject under discussion.
words.example: The lawyer asked only questions that were pertinent to the fraud charge.
words.mnemonic: It 'pertains' to the topic — pertinent things pertain directly to the matter.

words.definition: Sharing the same origin or ancestry, especially languages or words.
words.example: English 'mother' and German 'Mutter' are cognate, both descending from one ancient root.
words.mnemonic: co ('together') + gnate ('born', as in natal) — words born together from one family.

words.definition: Closely relevant and fitting to what is being considered.
words.example: Please keep your remarks germane to the agenda; we have no time for tangents.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'German' — picture a German cousin, a close relative of the topic (as in 'brothers-german').

words.definition: Most noticeable or prominent; standing out above the rest.
words.example: The analyst highlighted the report's salient points on the opening slide.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'salire', to leap — a salient fact leaps right out and grabs your eye.

words.definition: Greater in importance or rank than all others; supreme.
words.example: For any surgeon, the patient's safety is paramount and comes before everything else.
words.mnemonic: para + mount — positioned above the mountain, sitting at the very top.

words.definition: Crucially important in deciding how something develops or turns out.
words.example: Her testimony proved pivotal, swinging the whole jury toward acquittal.
words.mnemonic: Think 'pivot' — everything turns on it, the point the outcome spins around.

words.definition: Being the most perfect or typical example of a quality or kind.
words.example: With its checkered tablecloths and zinc bar, the café was the quintessential Parisian bistro.
words.mnemonic: quint ('fifth') + essence — the rarefied 'fifth essence', the purest distilled form of a thing.

words.definition: So small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.
words.example: The price gap between the two models was negligible, only a few cents.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'neglect' — small enough that you can safely neglect it.

words.definition: Not harmful or offensive; causing no injury or upset.
words.example: What seemed an innocuous comment somehow set off the entire family argument.
words.mnemonic: in ('not') + noc ('harm', as in noxious) — literally 'not harmful'.

words.definition: Small in importance or amount; at the edge rather than the center.
words.example: The expensive ad campaign had only a marginal effect on monthly sales.
words.mnemonic: Think 'margin' — scribbled out at the edge of the page, off to the side, not central.

words.definition: Existing in name only, or too small to matter much.
words.example: The museum charges a nominal fee of one dollar, barely enough to cover printing tickets.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'nomen' (name) — a nominal amount is real in name only.

words.definition: Large in amount, size, or importance.
words.example: After years of saving, she had a substantial sum in the bank.
words.mnemonic: It holds the word 'substance' — something substantial has real substance to it.

words.definition: Present in large quantities; more than enough.
words.example: The student took copious notes, filling three notebooks during one lecture.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'copy us' — imagine copies piling up in overwhelming heaps.

words.definition: Existing in very large quantities; plentiful.
words.example: Fish were so abundant in the lake that everyone caught their limit within an hour.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-bun-dant' — a bakery with so many buns they overflow the shelves.

words.definition: Available in very small amounts; hard to find.
words.example: During the drought, clean water became scarce and people waited hours in line.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'scare' — a scary shortage when there's barely any left.

words.definition: Thinly spread or scattered; not dense.
words.example: The old man's sparse hair barely covered his scalp.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spare' — only a spare bit, spread thin over a wide area.

words.definition: Lacking in quantity or quality; inadequate.
words.example: He tried to survive on the meager wages of a part-time job.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'meek' — a meek, tiny portion that leaves you still hungry.

words.definition: So small or trivial as to deserve contempt.
words.example: They offered a paltry ten dollars for a painting worth thousands.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'poultry' — a scrawny little chicken hardly worth the trouble.

words.definition: Enough or more than enough for a purpose.
words.example: The hall had ample room for all two hundred guests to dance.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'a full sample' — a generous, roomy helping.

words.definition: An overly large amount of something; an excess.
words.example: The new phone comes with a plethora of features that most people never use.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'plenty-thora' — plenty, and then a whole lot more.

words.definition: An amount left over after needs are met.
words.example: The farm produced a surplus of corn, so they sold the extra at market.
words.mnemonic: 'Sur-' means over (as in surcharge) plus more — an overage stacking up.

words.definition: The amount by which something falls short of what is needed.
words.example: The company ran a deficit this year, spending far more than it earned.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'deficient' — a deficit means you're short and lacking.

words.definition: A scarcity or lack of something.
words.example: There was a dearth of qualified applicants, so the position stayed open for months.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'earth' — picture barren earth yielding almost nothing.

words.definition: Smallness of number or quantity; scarcity.
words.example: The report suffered from a paucity of hard data to back its claims.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pauper-ity' — a pauper who owns very little.

words.definition: To exist or be present in very large numbers.
words.example: Rumors abound about who will be chosen as the next team captain.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'bound' — picture things bounding around everywhere, too many to count.
